title: What it took to voice a 1,000-line tank campaign with TTS, and why I ended up building a critic instead of a better generator
author: BinaryHelix
selftext:
I shipped Tanknado: Dead Signal this week, a tank-vs-horde campaign in three acts, on Android and the web. One person. The voices, music, art and much of the code are generated, and I want to share what that actually involved, because the generation was the easy part.

**Voices.** 1,091 crew clips plus 136 tutorial lines, text-to-speech with one reference voice per character. What mattered:
- Every take is transcribed and compared with its script line. A take that doesn't match goes on a retake list.
- Some lines fail every time. Very short barks, initials, and hyphenated numbers came out wrong again and again. The fix was editorial: after one retake, rewrite the line or cut it. Don't burn credits on the fifth take.
- Radio processing (band-limiting, squelch, static) does a lot to make TTS sit in a game mix. A clean studio voice over a tank engine sounds fake. The same voice on a radio sounds right.

**Judging.** The thing that improved the game most was an AI critic. It scored captured playthroughs of every chapter against a pass mark, and a release gate wouldn't ship a build until a whole capture round passed. Two lessons:
- Give the critic measurable checks: is the boss's tell visible on screen before it hits, is the HUD readable at phone size. Keep "is this fun" for yourself.
- The gate's own checks can flake. Camera-angle checks failed some rounds for no game reason, so a failed round gets read before anything else does.

**What I'd do differently:** write the voice lines for TTS from day one. Short lines, no abbreviations, numbers spelled the way they're said.

Act I is free with no ads, and plays in a browser if you want to hear the voices in context: https://tanknado.com/?utm_source=reddit&utm_campaign=aigamedev

What are others doing to keep one character's voice consistent across hundreds of lines?
